prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

In an attempt to bypass the sign problem in quantum Monte Carlo simulation of electronic systems within the framework of fixed node approach, we derive the exclusion principle "Two electrons can't be at the same external isopotential surface simultaneously" using the first postulate of quantum mechanics. We propose the exact Coulomb-Exchange nodal surface i.e. the exact boundary condition to solve the non-relativistic Schrodinger equation for the non-degenerate ground state of atoms and molecules. This boundary condition was applied to compute the ground state energies of N, Ne, Li2, Be2, B2, C2, N2, O2, F2, and H2O systems using diffusion Monte Carlo method. The ground state energies thus obtained agree well with the exact estimate of non-relativistic energies.

outputs.L1: To circumvent the sign problem in quantum Monte Carlo simulations of electronic systems within the fixed-node framework, we derive, from the first postulate of quantum mechanics, the exclusion principle that “two electrons cannot simultaneously occupy the same external isopotential surface.” We propose the exact Coulomb–exchange nodal surface—that is, the exact boundary condition for solving the nonrelativistic Schrödinger equation for the nondegenerate ground states of atoms and molecules. Using the diffusion Monte Carlo method, we apply this boundary condition to calculate the ground-state energies of N, Ne, Li₂, Be₂, B₂, C₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, and H₂O. The resulting ground-state energies agree well with exact estimates of the corresponding nonrelativistic energies.
outputs.L2: To circumvent the sign problem in quantum Monte Carlo simulations of electronic systems under the fixed-node framework, we use the first postulate of quantum mechanics to derive the following exclusion rule: two electrons cannot simultaneously occupy the same external isopotential surface. We then introduce the exact Coulomb–exchange nodal surface as the precise boundary condition for solving the nonrelativistic Schrödinger equation for nondegenerate atomic and molecular ground states. Using this boundary condition with the diffusion Monte Carlo method, we calculate ground-state energies for N, Ne, Li₂, Be₂, B₂, C₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, and H₂O. The resulting values closely match exact estimates of the corresponding nonrelativistic energies.
outputs.L3:
This work seeks to overcome the fermion sign problem in quantum Monte Carlo simulations by employing the fixed-node approach. It derives an exclusion principle according to which two electrons cannot simultaneously occupy the same external isopotential surface. On this basis, an exact Coulomb–exchange nodal surface is proposed as a boundary condition for solving the non-relativistic Schrödinger equation for non-degenerate ground states.

The proposed boundary condition is implemented in diffusion Monte Carlo calculations for a range of atomic and molecular systems, including N, Ne, Li₂, Be₂, B₂, C₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, and H₂O. The resulting ground-state energies show good agreement with benchmark estimates of exact non-relativistic energies, indicating that the Coulomb–exchange nodal-surface formulation may provide an accurate and effective way to control the sign problem in fixed-node quantum Monte Carlo calculations.
outputs.L4:
The fermion sign problem remains one of the central obstacles to accurate quantum Monte Carlo simulations of electronic systems. In fixed-node diffusion Monte Carlo, this difficulty is avoided by constraining the many-electron wave function to remain within regions separated by an assumed nodal surface, where the wave function vanishes. Although this procedure stabilizes the calculation, the resulting energy depends on the quality of the chosen nodes: an approximate nodal surface introduces a fixed-node error, while the exact nodal surface would produce the exact nonrelativistic ground-state energy within the adopted Hamiltonian.

The study develops an alternative theoretical basis for determining these nodes. Starting from the first postulate of quantum mechanics—the representation of a physical state by a wave function in Hilbert space—it derives an exclusion principle governing indistinguishable electrons. This formulation connects fermionic exclusion not only to the antisymmetry of the wave function under particle exchange, but also to the structure of the Coulomb interaction and the conditions under which electronic configurations must be excluded from the physically accessible state space.

On this basis, the authors propose a Coulomb-exchange nodal boundary condition for nondegenerate atomic and molecular ground states. The condition identifies the many-electron configurations at which the wave function must vanish as a consequence of electron exchange and Coulombic symmetry. It is presented as an exact boundary condition rather than as an empirical nodal approximation inherited from a trial wave function. If valid, it would remove or substantially reduce the main uncontrolled approximation in fixed-node quantum Monte Carlo.

The proposed nodal surface is tested through diffusion Monte Carlo calculations for a selection of atoms and molecules. Walkers are propagated in imaginary time while being constrained by the Coulomb-exchange boundary, allowing the ground-state energy to be projected without the instability normally caused by positive and negative fermionic amplitudes. The resulting total energies are compared with highly accurate nonrelativistic reference estimates.

Across the systems examined, the calculated ground-state energies closely agree with the best available exact or near-exact nonrelativistic values. This agreement indicates that the imposed boundary reproduces the physically relevant nodal structure with high accuracy. Because fixed-node diffusion Monte Carlo gives an upper bound to the exact ground-state energy under standard conditions, the small residual differences also provide a direct measure of the remaining nodal error.

The results therefore support both the practical accuracy and the broader theoretical significance of the Coulomb-exchange nodal surface. The work suggests that the fermion sign problem for nondegenerate atomic and molecular ground states may be addressed through a physically derived exclusion boundary rather than through system-specific optimization of approximate nodes. More broadly, it offers a possible route toward more reliable and less trial-function-dependent quantum Monte Carlo calculations of correlated electronic systems.
outputs.L5: Monte Carlo is a place where elegance, history, and excitement meet. Perched along the Mediterranean coast, it is famous for its grand casino, luxury yachts, and winding streets. Two visitors can experience the city in completely different ways: one may enjoy the glamour of the nightlife, while the other explores quiet gardens and scenic coastal views. Whether discovered through chance or careful planning, Monte Carlo leaves a lasting impression.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise abstract for a research paper proposing a Coulomb-Exchange nodal surface to address the fermion sign problem in fixed-node diffusion Monte Carlo calculations.
counterfactuals.output: The fermion sign problem limits the accuracy of diffusion Monte Carlo (DMC), where the fixed-node approximation makes the energy depend critically on the quality of a trial wave function’s nodal surface. We propose a Coulomb-Exchange (CX) nodal surface that incorporates electron exchange and Coulomb-driven correlation directly into the nodal constraint. The construction augments conventional determinant-based nodes with a compact, symmetry-preserving coordinate transformation derived from effective pairwise Coulomb-exchange interactions. It preserves antisymmetry, remains size consistent, and can be evaluated with polynomial computational cost. Fixed-node DMC calculations on representative atoms, molecules, and correlated model systems show reduced variational energies and smaller nodal errors relative to Hartree–Fock and standard multideterminant trial functions. The largest improvements occur in systems with near-degeneracy and strong exchange competition. These results establish the CX nodal surface as a practical route toward systematically improving fixed-node DMC without requiring prohibitively large determinant expansions.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a quantum chemistry study that derives the exclusion principle “Two electrons can't be at the same external isopotential surface simultaneously” and tests the resulting boundary condition on atoms and molecules.
counterfactuals.output:
The study proposes an additional electron-exclusion rule based on the external electrostatic potential \(v_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathbf r)\), rather than on spin and spatial coincidence. Its central claim is that an electronic wavefunction must satisfy

\[
\Psi(\ldots,\mathbf r_i,\ldots,\mathbf r_j,\ldots)=0
\quad\text{when}\quad
v_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathbf r_i)=v_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathbf r_j),
\]

meaning that two electrons cannot simultaneously lie on the same external equipotential surface. For atoms, whose nuclear potential is radial, this becomes a node at equal electron–nucleus distances, \(r_i=r_j\). For molecules, the corresponding nodal boundary follows the generally non-spherical equipotential surfaces generated by all nuclei.

The authors derive this condition from their treatment of the many-electron Schrödinger equation and incorporate it into trial wavefunctions as an explicit nodal or correlation factor. They then test the constrained wavefunctions on representative atoms and molecules, comparing calculated energies and related electronic properties with conventional quantum-chemical results. The reported calculations are intended to show that enforcing the new boundary condition can capture part of electron correlation and provide workable approximations across both atomic and molecular systems.

Conceptually, the proposal is much stronger than the standard Pauli exclusion principle. Pauli antisymmetry forces a same-spin wavefunction to vanish when two electrons occupy the same spatial point; it does not forbid opposite-spin electrons—or electrons at different points—from having the same value of the external potential. Accordingly, the study is best understood as proposing and numerically testing a nonstandard nodal ansatz, not as establishing a generally accepted exclusion principle. In particular, ordinary correlated wavefunctions can have nonzero amplitude when two electrons lie at different positions on the same equipotential surface, so the universality of the claimed boundary condition would require evidence beyond favorable variational tests.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an academic abstract explaining how the first postulate of quantum mechanics can be used to obtain an exact nodal surface for non-degenerate electronic ground states.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract—**The first postulate of quantum mechanics identifies a pure electronic state with a ray in the many-electron Hilbert space. For a fixed-nuclei Hamiltonian with a non-degenerate ground state, this ray is unique; consequently, any representative ground-state wavefunction differs only by a nonzero scalar or global phase, which leaves its zero set invariant. Starting from an antisymmetric trial state \(\Phi\) with nonzero ground-state overlap, imaginary-time projection yields
\[
\Psi_0 \propto \lim_{\tau\to\infty} e^{-\tau \hat H}\Phi .
\]
The exact nodal set is therefore
\[
\mathcal N_0=\{\mathbf R:\Psi_0(\mathbf R)=0\},
\]
with the nodal surface defined, apart from lower-dimensional singularities, as the codimension-one boundary separating regions of opposite sign. For real, time-reversal-invariant electronic Hamiltonians, \(\Psi_0\) may be chosen real, making this sign-domain interpretation explicit. Non-degeneracy is essential because it removes basis-dependent mixing among ground states and renders the nodal set uniquely associated with the physical state. Thus, the first postulate establishes the representation and phase invariance needed for an exact nodal surface, while the Hamiltonian and ground-state projection determine that surface in practice. The postulate alone does not provide its geometry; rather, it guarantees that the nodes extracted from the exact non-degenerate ground-state ray are physically unambiguous.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe a method for computing non-relativistic ground-state energies of N, Ne, Li2, Be2, B2, C2, N2, O2, F2, and H2O using diffusion Monte Carlo while bypassing the sign problem.
counterfactuals.output:
A practical way to obtain these energies is **all-electron fixed-node diffusion Monte Carlo (FN-DMC)**. The fixed-node constraint avoids the exponential fermion sign problem by turning the calculation into positive-probability diffusion within nodal pockets.

### Procedure

1. **Specify the non-relativistic Hamiltonian**
   For clamped nuclei,
   \[
   H=-\frac12\sum_i\nabla_i^2
   -\sum_{iA}\frac{Z_A}{r_{iA}}
   +\sum_{i<j}\frac1{r_{ij}}
   +\sum_{A<B}\frac{Z_AZ_B}{R_{AB}} .
   \]
   Use all electrons and no scalar-relativistic, spin-orbit, or finite-nuclear-mass corrections. For molecules, either use prescribed geometries or minimize the DMC energy with respect to bond lengths and the H–O–H angle.

2. **Construct an antisymmetric trial function**
   Use a Slater–Jastrow or multideterminant Slater–Jastrow form,
   \[
   \Psi_T(\mathbf R)=e^{J(\mathbf R)}
   \sum_k c_kD_k^\uparrow D_k^\downarrow .
   \]
   Determinants can be obtained from Hartree–Fock, CASSCF, or selected-CI/CIPSI calculations. Include the proper spatial and spin symmetry for each atom or molecule. The Jastrow factor should satisfy electron–electron and electron–nucleus cusp conditions; orbital rotations, determinant coefficients, and Jastrow parameters are optimized using variational Monte Carlo. Backflow transformations may further improve the nodes.

3. **Apply fixed-node imaginary-time projection**
   DMC projects
   \[
   \Psi(\tau)=e^{-\tau(H-E_T)}\Psi_T
   \]
   toward the lowest state compatible with the nodal surface of \(\Psi_T\). Importance-sample the mixed distribution
   \[
   f(\mathbf R,\tau)=\Psi_T(\mathbf R)\Psi(\mathbf R,\tau)
   \]
   using drift, diffusion, and branching controlled by the local energy
   \[
   E_L(\mathbf R)=\frac{H\Psi_T(\mathbf R)}{\Psi_T(\mathbf R)}.
   \]

4. **Bypass the sign problem with the nodal constraint**
   Walkers are forbidden from crossing surfaces where \(\Psi_T=0\). Consequently, each nodal pocket has a nonnegative distribution and can be sampled as a standard branching diffusion process. This removes the exponential cancellation of positive and negative walkers. The resulting energy
   \[
   E_{\rm FN}=
   \frac{\langle\Psi_T|H|\Psi_{\rm FN}\rangle}
        {\langle\Psi_T|\Psi_{\rm FN}\rangle}
   \]
   is an upper bound to the exact energy for the chosen symmetry. The remaining bias is the **fixed-node error**, not a statistical sign problem.

5. **Control numerical errors**
   Run several small time steps and extrapolate to zero time step; increase walker populations to check population-control bias; equilibrate thoroughly; and accumulate independent blocks for statistical uncertainties. Repeat calculations with successively larger multideterminant expansions or backflow. A lowering of the FN-DMC energy indicates improved nodes.

6. **Calculate the requested systems**
   Perform separate symmetry-appropriate calculations for N, Ne, Li\(_2\), Be\(_2\), B\(_2\), C\(_2\), N\(_2\), O\(_2\), F\(_2\), and H\(_2\)O. Open-shell atoms and molecules require the correct spin multiplicity—for example, triplet O\(_2\)—and weakly bound or multireference systems such as Be\(_2\), B\(_2\), and C\(_2\) generally need multideterminant nodes.

This method gives statistically exact projection **within the imposed nodes**. It does not solve the unrestricted fermion problem exactly unless the trial nodal surface is exact, but it bypasses the practical sign problem and provides variational ground-state energy estimates.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a research-paper abstract about applying an exact Coulomb-Exchange boundary condition within the fixed-node approach and comparing the calculated molecular energies with exact non-relativistic estimates.
counterfactuals.output: We investigate the incorporation of an exact Coulomb–exchange boundary condition into the fixed-node quantum Monte Carlo framework for molecular electronic-structure calculations. The boundary condition enforces the correct short-range behavior associated with electron–electron Coulomb interactions and fermionic exchange, thereby constraining the trial wave function in regions where conventional parametrizations may introduce significant local errors. Molecular ground-state energies are obtained using systematically optimized antisymmetric trial functions and are compared with the best available exact non-relativistic, clamped-nuclei estimates. The Coulomb–exchange constraint improves the consistency and stability of the fixed-node calculations while preserving the variational character of the resulting energies. Across the benchmark systems considered, the calculated energies closely approach reference values, with residual discrepancies attributable primarily to nodal-surface errors rather than imperfect cusp behavior or basis-set limitations. These results clarify the role of exact local boundary conditions in separating short-range correlation effects from the global fixed-node approximation and provide a practical route toward more accurate and transferable quantum Monte Carlo descriptions of molecules.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
